content: Acid indigestion, also known as dyspepsia, is a condition characterized by an excessive amount of hydrochloric acid in the stomach. Chronic acid indigestion can irritate the stomach lining or the duodenum, potentially leading to ulcers, which may become life-threatening. However, it is important to note that 85-95% of stomach ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori infection rather than excessive stomach acidity. Acid indigestion should not be confused with heartburn, which typically involves irritation of the esophagus. Causes of Acid Indigestion Common causes include: Consumption of fatty or spicy foods. Excessive intake of alcohol or caffeine. Smoking. Overeating or eating late at night, especially just before sleeping. Certain medications and conditions can also contribute to acid indigestion, such as: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Specific medications like atazanavir, duloxetine, or lithium. Conditions like primary hyperparathyroidism, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), or Helicobacter pylori infection. Historical Perspective Acid indigestion was first described in the 1980s as discomfort in the epigastric or retrosternal regions related to the gastrointestinal system. Patients were categorized into subtypes based on symptoms and underlying mechanisms, such as reflux-like, ulcer-like, dysmotility-like, or unspecified dyspepsia. Reflux-like dyspepsia is often considered part of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) unless proven otherwise. Classification According to the Rome II classification, acid indigestion can be divided into: 1. Ulcer-like dyspepsia: Characterized by significant upper abdominal pain. 2. Dysmotility-like dyspepsia: Symptoms include early satiety, bloating, or nausea. 3. Unspecified dyspepsia: Symptoms that do not fit into the above categories. Pathophysiology The exact mechanisms of acid indigestion remain under investigation. Contributing factors include: Gastrointestinal motor abnormalities, such as delayed gastric emptying or irregular gastric rhythms. Altered visceral sensation, with increased sensitivity to minor stimuli in both fasting and postprandial states. Psychosocial factors, including anxiety, which may exacerbate symptoms. Helicobacter pylori infection plays a significant role in some cases, and genetic predisposition may also contribute, though evidence is limited. Post-infectious causes, such as bacterial or viral gastroenteritis, have also been implicated. Differentiating Acid Indigestion from Other Diseases Acid indigestion must be distinguished from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as: Peptic ulcers. GERD. Biliary tract disease. Pancreatitis. Gastric cancer. Medication-induced dyspepsia. A thorough patient history and diagnostic tests, such as endoscopy, are essential for accurate differentiation. Epidemiology and Demographics Acid indigestion affects individuals across all age groups, though studies often focus on adults over 18. Peak prevalence varies by population, with higher rates observed in middle-aged individuals. There is no clear gender or racial predilection, though some studies suggest women and certain ethnic groups, such as African-Americans and Chinese, may be at higher risk. Risk Factors Key risk factors include: Excessive alcohol consumption. Smoking. Overuse of medications like aspirin or antidepressants. Psychosocial factors, such as anxiety or somatization. Diagnosis Diagnosis is made after ruling out other potential causes. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is often performed to exclude structural abnormalities or malignancies. Additional tests, such as nutrient meal tests or imaging studies, may be used to assess gastric motility and visceral sensitivity. Symptoms Common symptoms include: Epigastric pain. Nausea and vomiting. Upper abdominal fullness or bloating. Anxiety and distress. Less common symptoms include acidic taste, belching, and heartburn. Physical Examination Most patients appear normal on physical examination, though epigastric tenderness may be present. Additional assessments, such as stool analysis or oral cavity examination, may help identify underlying causes like GERD or biliary tract disease. Laboratory Findings There are no specific laboratory findings for acid indigestion. However, tests such as complete blood count (CBC), liver function tests, and urea breath tests for H. pylori may be performed based on clinical suspicion. Treatment Treatment focuses on symptom relief and improving overall health. Key approaches include: Dietary modifications, such as reducing fat intake and avoiding trigger foods. Pharmacological therapy, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), H2 receptor antagonists, and antidepressants for psychological symptoms. Eradication of H. pylori infection when present. Treatment plans should be individualized based on patient needs, socioeconomic factors, and preferences. Prevention Preventive measures include: Avoiding trigger foods and beverages, such as those high in fat, spice, or acidity. Reducing alcohol and caffeine consumption. Quitting smoking. Practicing good sleep hygiene. Surgery Surgical intervention is rarely indicated for acid indigestion and is reserved for severe or refractory cases.
